sentences.text: The gull put things on the third bollard from the steps, and only on the third.
Nobody knew why the third.
It was not the biggest or the nearest or the one that got the sun.
It was a bollard exactly like the four on either side of it, cast iron, painted white about nine times, with a chip out of the top where somebody's rope had been.
Things appeared on it.
Not often — four or five times a year, no more — and always overnight, and always after weather.
A green plastic torch.
A single earring, gold, bent.
A tobacco tin with somebody's initials scratched in it that turned out to be nobody's initials anybody recognised.
A watch that did not go.
A folding knife with the blade rusted open.
A hair slide with two of the four stones missing.
And, since before Nél was born, the small blue shoe.
There was a book, as well, though nobody called it a book.
It was a school exercise book in the harbourmaster's office with a list in four or five different handwritings: the date, what had appeared, and whether it had gone.
It started in 1974, which was when somebody had finally thought to start it, and it had five pages used.
Nél had read the whole thing in an afternoon when she was ten, standing up, because she had not been exactly given permission.
*14.xi.81 — spectacles, one arm missing.
Claimed 19.xi by Sr.
Bento.* *3.iii.86 — small anchor, brass, ornamental.
Not claimed.* *22.ix.94 — mobile telephone.
Not claimed (obviously).* The *(obviously)* had been added in different ink, later, by somebody with a sense of humour.
The shoe was the only one that had ever stayed.
Everything else got claimed, usually within a week, usually by somebody who came down and stood in front of the bollard for a while first.
The standing in front of it was not a formality and nobody had ever decided it should happen.
It simply did.
A thing appeared, word went round the harbour by lunchtime, and over the following days people came down and looked at it, one at a time, and most of them went away again.
Nél watched four claimings before she was twelve and they were all the same shape.
The person would come down the steps and along the wall and stop, and they would not touch it at first.
There would be a pause of about a minute in which they did not touch it.
Then they would pick it up and turn it over once and put it in a pocket and walk back up the steps, and that would be the whole of it.
Nobody ever announced anything.
Nobody ever said *that's mine*.
Somebody would ask Dona Lurdes the next day and she would say *the earring's gone*, and that was how the harbour found out.
The tobacco tin went to a man from Cabo who did not explain himself.
The torch went back to a boy in Nél's own class who had dropped it off the ferry and had been shouted at about it.
The shoe had been on that bollard, more or less, for seventy years.
There were three photographs of it that Nél knew about.
One from a newspaper in 1979, in an article about the town that got almost everything else wrong.
One taken by a Dutch couple in about 2004 and put on the internet, where it had attracted thirteen comments, all of them from people inventing worse versions of the story.
And one on the wall of the café, black and white, from some time in the sixties, in which the shoe is on the bollard and there is a boy in the background who is now a man who runs the chandlery.
It was not always on the bollard.
People had moved it.
It had been in the harbourmaster's office, in a drawer, for a while in the nineteen-eighties.
It had been on a shelf in the café.
It had been, for one summer, in a small glass box which everybody agreed afterwards had been a mistake.
Every time, within a year or two, somebody had quietly put it back out on the third bollard, because that was where it went.
